wine.name: Treinta y Dos Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, from ungrafted vines planted in 1932.
wine.sites: The old vineyard planted in 1932 that the house took on in 2004, a small plot at Mainqué in the Alto Valle, on its own roots and farmed biodynamically.
wine.making: Fermented with native yeasts and a share of whole bunches, in concrete vats and in some vintages partly in barrel. The wine is then aged in concrete vats and used French oak barrels, with no new wood since the 2013 vintage by one account, for nine months to about nineteen by vintage.
wine.glass: Pale ruby; crushed raspberry, wild strawberry, red cherry and rose over rosehip and a stony, almost tile like note; light in body and taut, with gentle, fine grained tannin, bright acidity and a long, fine finish.
wine.ageing: Pretty when young, it has the structure to keep, and a strong vintage gains for ten years and more.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, a short airing will do; a Burgundy glass.

records.table: Named for 1932, the year its ungrafted vines went in at Mainqué in the Río Negro valley, Treinta y Dos is Bodega Chacra's Pinot Noir. Pale, taut and scented with raspberry and rose, it calls for a Burgundy glass at cool cellar temperature.
records.story: Pinot Noir was planted at Mainqué, in the Alto Valle of the Río Negro, in 1932, and it stayed on its own roots: the desert around the valley is credited with keeping phylloxera away. By the turn of the century the vineyard had been abandoned and gave little fruit. A member of the Tuscan family behind Sassicaia came to the valley, worked a vintage beside a Danish born winemaker there, and in 2004 took on the old vineyard, first on a lease. As the house tells it, the owner would not sell, so little did the vines yield, until a bottle of the first wine from them won him over. That wine was named Treinta y Dos, thirty two, for the year of planting. Two more old Pinot Noir sites followed, one planted in 1955, which gave Cincuenta y Cinco, and one of 1967, and a new block was later planted with cuttings from the vines of 1932 and 1955. The house farmed biodynamically, certified within five years by its own account, and made its preparations on the estate. Treinta y Dos showed that Argentina had a Pinot Noir of old vines and fine bones, far from Mendoza and its Malbec, and it remains the bottle that makes that argument.

wine.sites: The Finca Milagros vineyard in the Alto Valle near General Roca, planted with Sémillon in 1942 and farmed for its old vines.

records.table: From Sémillon planted in 1942 in the Finca Milagros vineyard near General Roca, Humberto Canale makes its Old Vineyard Sémillon. Fig, melon and honeysuckle over a waxy texture and lively acidity: pour it cool, beside fish or white meat.
records.story: The house carries the name of its founder, a civil engineer who came to Buenos Aires from Genoa. In 1909, by his family's account brought south by one of his engineering professors, he chose the Alto Valle of the Río Negro near General Roca for a vineyard. The valley had only lately been opened to settlers after the Conquest of the Desert, and canals from the river were turning dry land into farms. His family credits him with bringing the grapes that would mark the house, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Sémillon among them. The winery has stayed in the family ever since: four generations have run it, a great nephew of the founder among them. In 1937 Riesling was planted in the La Morita vineyard, and in 1942 Sémillon in the vineyard called Finca Milagros; those vines feed the Old Vineyard range, which the house presents as a tribute to its old family vineyards. The Sémillon matters because it is old vine Sémillon from a valley better known for apples and pears and, lately, for Pinot Noir: a wine that carries the long memory of the Alto Valle in a glass.

wine.name: Noemía
wine.grapes: Malbec alone, from ungrafted vines planted in 1932.
wine.sites: A small single vineyard at Mainqué in the Alto Valle, planted in 1932 on its own roots from a massal selection and farmed organically.
wine.making: Fermented with native yeasts, in open oak vats with a share of whole bunches in some vintages. The wine is then aged for about eighteen months by most accounts, twenty three in one vintage, in large casks of 600 litres since the late 2010s and in French oak barrels before.
wine.glass: Blackberry, black cherry and dark currant over rose petal, mint and a stony note; creamy and full yet fresh, with fine, ripe tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Generous when young, it keeps its fruit and fine tannin for a decade and more in a strong vintage.

records.table: Bodega Noemía bottles its flagship Malbec under the house's own name, Noemía, from vines on their own roots, planted at Mainqué in 1932. Dark fruited and creamy, lifted by rose petal and mint, it opens after an hour in a decanter and belongs in a Bordeaux glass.
records.story: As the house tells it, an Italian countess and a Danish born winemaker who were working in the Alto Valle of the Río Negro came upon a neglected plot of Malbec at Mainqué. It had been planted in 1932 and had stayed on its own roots as the decades passed; they saw what it was, and set out to make a little wine from it, almost for fun. Bodega Noemía was born of it in 2001. Each vine, the house says, is genetically distinct, a field of old Malbec rather than a single clone. The founders restored the vineyard and farmed it organically, later with certification, and they built the rest of their range on grapes from growers of Mainqué, held on long leases. Noemía, from the vines of 1932, became the house's flagship, with J. Alberto and A Lisa beside it. The wine changed how Patagonian Malbec was seen: dense and dark, yet with the freshness and fine bones of a cool, windy and low valley, rather than the sun of Luján de Cuyo or the altitude of the Uco Valley. Mendoza's Malbec country lies far to the north; this is the grape keeping its poise a long way south of it.

records.table: A dinosaur found as the winery was built at San Patricio del Chañar, in Neuquén, gave Familia Schroeder the name of its Saurus range, and Saurus Pinot Noir is the range's red. Cherry, plum and rose, round and fresh, it likes a slight chill.
records.story: Familia Schroeder was founded in 2001 by a businessman of a family of German origin, among the pioneers who planted vines in the irrigated desert of San Patricio del Chañar, in Neuquén. Early in the building of the winery the works turned up fossil bones: the remains of a plant eating dinosaur some seventy five million years old, by the house's account. Palaeontologists were called in for the long work of extraction, and when the species was described in 2010 it was named Panamericansaurus schroederi, for the Schroeder family and for the energy company that backed the dig. The house built a cellar over the place of the find, where the bones can be seen as they were found, and it named its first range of wines, and its restaurant, Saurus. Its first wine was a Saurus Select Pinot Noir of the 2003 vintage, and Pinot Noir became the grape the house is known for, made in several styles, a late harvest wine among them. The Saurus Pinot Noir is the bottle a guest is most likely to meet on a list, and its story fits in a sentence: a Patagonian Pinot Noir from a cellar built over a dinosaur.

records.table: At San Patricio del Chañar in Neuquén, Bodega del Fin del Mundo ages Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot apart in French oak, then blends them as Special Blend, its flagship red. Dark fruited and supple, it goes beside red meat after a spell in a decanter.
records.story: San Patricio del Chañar, north of the city of Neuquén, was dry steppe until the late 1990s, when river water was brought to the desert to plant vines on a large scale. Bodega del Fin del Mundo was founded there in 1999, the project of the developer behind the zone's planting, and its first vineyards went in that year. The first harvest came in 2002, and the house has made its wines at San Patricio del Chañar ever since, as the pioneer of the zone. Others followed it into the desert, Familia Schroeder among them, and the zone grew into the modern centre of Neuquén's wine, as the Alto Valle of the Río Negro is its historic one. The house planted the grapes of Bordeaux beside Malbec, and the Special Blend, a blend of Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, became its flagship. Each grape spends its first months in barrel on its own before the blend is chosen. The wine shows that Patagonia's desert, warm by day and cold by night, can ripen Cabernet Sauvignon and Malbec into a deep red that keeps its freshness, a long way from the Bordeaux blends of Mendoza.

others.note: A red of the house's Gran Reserva level, as its own technical sheet shows.

traps: Bodega del Fin del Mundo is in Neuquén, at San Patricio del Chañar, not at the southern tip of Argentina, whatever its name suggests.
The Special Blend is a blend of Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, not a varietal Malbec.

cards.front: Bodega del Fin del Mundo: which grapes make its Special Blend?
cards.back: Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon in roughly equal parts, with Merlot.

cards.front: In which year did Bodega del Fin del Mundo make its first harvest?
cards.back: 2002, after its first vines were planted at San Patricio del Chañar in 1999.

questions.q: A guest asks how the Special Blend of Bodega del Fin del Mundo is put together. Which answer fits?
opts: Each grape is aged apart in oak, then blended and returned to barrel
The grapes are fermented together in one vat and bottled young
Malbec alone is aged in old casks for five years
The wine is blended from purchased Mendoza wines
questions.exp: Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot are aged apart in French oak before the blend is chosen, then the blend goes back to barrel; it is not a co-fermented young wine.

questions.q: In which year was Bodega del Fin del Mundo founded at San Patricio del Chañar?
questions.exp: The house was founded and planted its first vines in 1999, with a first harvest in 2002; 1909 is the founding of Humberto Canale in the Río Negro valley.

report: Founded 1999 rests on Mercado (founded in 1999) and ANBariloche (first plantings in 1999); the house's own site says it has made wine since 2002, the first harvest, which Wine Folly also gives.

Older labels read Special Blend Reserva and a 2019 listing Special Red Blend; the record uses Special Blend, the plan's words, and teaches the blend of about two fifths Malbec, two fifths Cabernet Sauvignon and a fifth Merlot that a critic's listings give for 2006, 2010 and 2019 and a merchant's sheet confirms.
The barrel regime of eight months apart and fifteen more blended rests on one review of the 2012; a second source confirms only ageing in oak in two steps, so the record keeps it to one vintage.
The founder is not named: no source found says he has died, and his family later left the house for a separate bodega, which rests on one source and is left out.
The present owner is volatile and is not named; a provincial plan of 1996 to irrigate the zone rests on one source and is told only as river water brought to the desert.

changed: story: was founded by a businessman who saw a new wine region; vintages from 2003 onward; now the project of the developer behind the zone's planting; the vintage cut, Vinous and Patagonia.com.ar tie the house to the zone's developer; the first vintage of the Special Blend was found in no source.

others: was Gran Reserva beneath the Special Blend; a Reserva Cabernet Sauvignon; now the Gran Reserva alone, as its technical sheet shows, the rank of the levels and the Reserva Cabernet were in no source read.
sources[2]: was ANBariloche; now Interpatagonia, the second source for the first harvest of 2002 and the pioneer.
sources[3]: was Firstleaf; now Vinous, for the developer behind the zone; the blend rests on Social Vignerons and a critic's listing for 2019.
open: The barrel regime of eight months apart and fifteen blended is one vintage's and is kept to that in the making.
The house later passed to a business group that is not named; told nowhere in the record.
